title: A Kepler ellipse, RECORDED: the dataset is the experiment's lab book
abstract: 20. A Kepler ellipse, RECORDED: the dataset is the experiment's lab book. A true two-body problem (an anchored body exerts no gravity here, by design - walls must not attract). Sun mass 3, planet mass 1, G = 1, so the RELATIVE orbit has mu = G(M+m) = 4. Starting at perihelion separation r_p = a(1-e) = 1 with a = 2.5, e = 0.6, the relative vis-viva speed is sqrt(mu(2/r_p - 1/a)) = sqrt(6.4). Split about the stationary centre of mass: planet gets 3/4 of it, sun 1/4 backwards. Aphelion separation must be a(1+e) = 4, and the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(a^3/mu) = 12.418264743622237. The dataset records one full period; a SELF-JOIN of the states table then measures the separation extremes - the database answers the physics question.
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `sun` | `sphere` | `mass = 3`, `radius = 0.15`, `position = [-0.25, 0, 0]`, `velocity = [0, -0.6324555320336759, 0]` |
| `planet` | `sphere` | `mass = 1`, `radius = 0.05`, `position = [0.75, 0, 0]`, `velocity = [0, 1.8973665961010276, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`sphere`** — a uniform solid ball. `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`radius`** — the radius, in metres.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`velocity`** — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is ON**, with `G = 1`. Every pair of bodies attracts every other by `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`, softened at short range if `softening` is set.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
eom:
There are 2 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = F_grav_i

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `F_grav_i = sum over j != i of G m_i m_j (x_j - x_i) / |x_j - x_i|^3` — the mutual attraction, softened at short range if `softening` is set
constraints:
**This model has no joints.** Nothing algebraic relates the coordinates, so the system is an ordinary differential equation rather than a differential-algebraic one, and it needs no Lagrange multipliers and no constraint Jacobian.

That does not mean nothing is conserved. Energy, linear momentum and angular momentum are still exact consequences of the equations of motion, and comparing them before and after a run is the honest way to judge the integration.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 2 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
2 bodies x 13 numbers = 26 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

There are no algebraic constraints, so the whole of the mechanics above is one first-order system

```
dy/dt = f(t, y),   y in R^26
```

handed to the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

The right-hand side `f` unpacks `y` into bodies, computes every force and torque, and packs the derivatives back in the same 13-per-body order.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`set system.g_constant = 1` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `1`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`new sphere` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid ball**, named `sun`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 3` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.15` — the radius, in metres.
- `position = [-0.25, 0, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `velocity = [0, -0.6324555320336759, 0]` — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.

---

`new sphere` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid ball**, named `planet`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.05` — the radius, in metres.
- `position = [0.75, 0, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `velocity = [0, 1.8973665961010276, 0]` — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.
steps.code:
sim.do("new sphere as sun    { mass = 3, radius = 0.15, position = [-0.25, 0, 0], velocity = [0, -0.6324555320336759, 0] }")
sim.do("new sphere as planet { mass = 1, radius = 0.05, position = [0.75, 0, 0], velocity = [0, 1.8973665961010276, 0] }")

steps.title: Choose the integrator
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`method adams` chooses the time integrator. The form is `METHOD <adams|bdf|sprk|ida>`.

Here it selects the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

All stepping in this simulator goes through the vendored pure-Rust SUNDIALS translation. There is no hand-written Euler or Verlet anywhere.

steps.title: Integrate
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`run 12.418264743622237` advances the simulation by **12.418264743622237 seconds of duration** — not to absolute time 12.418264743622237. This trips people up: `run 1.7` followed by `run 2.89` leaves you at t = 4.59, not at 2.89. The form is `RUN <duration> [STEPS <n>]`.

`steps 200` asks for the result to be reported at 200 equally spaced points across that interval. It does not set the integrator's internal step size — SUNDIALS chooses that itself from the error tolerances, and takes as many internal steps between reports as accuracy demands.

This is the cell that actually integrates, so it is the slow one. It prints the time reached and how many internal solver steps were needed.

steps.title: Interrogate the dataset with SQL
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> perihelion and aphelion of the SEPARATION, asked of the DATABASE:
> a self-join pairs the two bodies frame by frame.

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`sql "SELECT MIN(sqrt((p.x-s.x)*(p.x-s.x) + (p.y-s.y)*(p.y-s.y))) AS perihelion, MAX(sqrt((p.x-s.x)*(p.x-s.x) + (p.y-s.y)*(p.y-s.y))) AS aphelion FROM states p JOIN states s ON s.frame = p.frame WHERE p.body = (SELECT body FROM bodies WHERE name = 'planet') AND s.body = (SELECT body FROM bodies WHERE name = 'sun')"` — a command of the simulator's language. Sent as typed; the simulator prints whatever it has to say about it.
steps.code: sim.do("sql \"SELECT MIN(sqrt((p.x-s.x)*(p.x-s.x) + (p.y-s.y)*(p.y-s.y))) AS perihelion, MAX(sqrt((p.x-s.x)*(p.x-s.x) + (p.y-s.y)*(p.y-s.y))) AS aphelion FROM states p JOIN states s ON s.frame = p.frame WHERE p.body = (SELECT body FROM bodies WHERE name = 'planet') AND s.body = (SELECT body FROM bodies WHERE name = 'sun')\"")

steps.title: Interrogate the dataset with SQL (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> the centre of mass never moves, and the energy ledger stays flat

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`sql "SELECT MAX(ABS(comx)) AS com_x, MAX(ABS(comy)) AS com_y, MAX(energy) - MIN(energy) AS energy_spread FROM frames"` — a command of the simulator's language. Sent as typed; the simulator prints whatever it has to say about it.
steps.code: sim.do("sql \"SELECT MAX(ABS(comx)) AS com_x, MAX(ABS(comy)) AS com_y, MAX(energy) - MIN(energy) AS energy_spread FROM frames\"")

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- The values printed above are the result. Read them against the physical expectations set out earlier in this notebook.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.
